title: Data breach
text: Over the weekend someone copied your customer database. They have sent a sample to prove it.

opts.label: Disclose now
opts.hint: Tell customers and regulators today; pay for monitoring.

out.text: Customers respect the candour. Most stay.
A class action is filed anyway.

opts.label: Investigate quietly first
opts.hint: Find out how bad it is before saying anything.

out.text: It was contained. You disclose a small incident.
It leaks before you are ready.
It disappears.
The attackers sell the data anyway, and the story of the cover-up with it.

lesson: In a breach the first loss is data; the second, larger one is trust. Preparation shifts the odds and disclosure limits the second loss.

title: {person} is resigning
text: Your {role} has asked for ten minutes and closed the door. There is an offer from elsewhere, and it is a good one.

opts.label: Counter-offer
opts.hint: A raise and a retention bonus, today.

out.text: They stay.
They thank you and leave anyway.
A gracious exit.
They leave, bitterly, and everyone hears about it.

lesson: Counter-offers buy time more often than loyalty. A bench of successors turns a resignation from a crisis into an inconvenience.

title: The auditors have questions
text: Your auditors have found revenue recognised a quarter early in two regions. They want to know whether it is a pattern.

opts.label: Restate openly
opts.hint: Correct the accounts and say so.

out.text: A painful announcement, then closure.
The auditors accept it.
A whistleblower writes to the regulator.
The market draws its own conclusions.

lesson: Accounting credibility is binary. Once investors doubt one number they discount all of them.

title: The account is empty
text: Payroll is due on Friday and there is not enough in the bank to cover it.

opts.label: Emergency share sale
opts.hint: Sell a quarter of the company at half its value.

out.text: The wire arrives on Thursday.
Money, at a price.

opts.label: Sell your receivables
opts.hint: A factor pays 85 cents on the dollar for most of your unpaid invoices.

out.text: Cash today for cash you were owed tomorrow.
Some wait. Many do not.

lesson: Insolvency is a cash event, not a profit event. Every option now is expensive because you are negotiating without alternatives — the cheap ones were available two quarters ago.

title: Covenant breach
text: You have broken a condition of {loan}. The bank’s workout team has replaced your usual contact.

opts.label: Pay for a waiver
opts.hint: A 1.5% fee and 1.5 points more interest.

out.text: The bank grants three quarters of relief.

opts.label: Equity cure
opts.hint: Sell 12% of the company at a discount and pay down 40% of the loan.

out.text: The covenant is cured with shareholders’ money.

opts.label: Dare them to call it
opts.hint: They do not want the keys.

out.text: They blink.
They demand half the loan back at once.

lesson: Covenants are tripwires that hand control to the lender before the money runs out. Watch the headroom on the Capital page, not just the cash balance.

title: Walkout in {city}
text: Most of your {city} staff have stopped work. They want to talk to you, not to their manager.

opts.label: Emergency raises
opts.hint: Ten points against market, in that office.

out.text: They go back to work.

opts.label: Listen, then change things
opts.hint: A town hall and real commitments.

out.text: They believe you.
They have heard it before. One in seven resign.
Three in ten are fired. The rest of the company watches.

lesson: A walkout is the end of a long process of not being heard. Morale and pay trends told you this was coming.

title: Your supplier is in the news
text: A documentary has filmed conditions inside the offshore factory that makes most of your inputs.

opts.label: Cut them off
opts.hint: Drop the supplier today and pay for emergency supply.

out.text: Expensive, immediate, and seen to be done.
Nobody believes the audit.

lesson: The price was low because the risk was yours. Supply-chain reputation risk does not appear in any quote.

title: A boycott is trending
text: A decision you made months ago has been picked up by campaigners. The hashtag has your name in it.

out.text: It ends within a week.
Some people are persuaded.
The statement is quoted mockingly for a month.
It burns out, slowly.

lesson: Reputation is a balance you draw on in a crisis. Companies with a full account are given the benefit of the doubt; the rest are not.

title: What the sellers did not mention
text: Three months after closing, a liability has surfaced in the business you bought in {city}: about {amount} that was never in the data room.

opts.label: Pay it and move on
opts.hint: Settle and write the lesson down.

out.text: The cheque is written; part of the goodwill is written off.
You recover most of it.
The sellers have spent the money. You pay the liability and your lawyers.

lesson: Due diligence is cheap compared with what it finds. The seller always knows more than the buyer; the price should assume so.

title: The board has lost patience
text: Your investors now own most of the company, and the losses are not shrinking. The lead director asks for an hour, alone.

opts.label: Present a turnaround plan
opts.hint: Convince them you know the way back.

out.text: They give you four more quarters.
They have heard plans before.

opts.label: Make the cuts they want
opts.hint: One job in ten, everywhere, now.

out.text: The board is satisfied. The company is not.
They back down.
It is not your company.

lesson: Every funding round sells some control. Below half the votes, a founder serves at the board’s pleasure — and boards run out of pleasure after enough losing quarters.

title: Food-safety scare
text: Several customers of your {city} location have reported food poisoning. A local reporter is calling.

opts.label: Close, clean, and say so
opts.hint: Shut for a week, bring in inspectors, publish the results.

out.text: Painful, and trusted.
It was a supplier problem elsewhere.
It was you. It is on the evening news.

lesson: In consumer businesses trust is the product. Fast, visible action limits the damage; hoping it goes away multiplies it.

title: The main press has failed
text: The largest machine in your {city} plant has cracked a frame. The manufacturer quotes ten weeks for a replacement part.

opts.label: Pay for an emergency rebuild
opts.hint: A specialist crew, flown in, working nights.

out.text: Back in two weeks, at a price.

opts.label: Outsource production meanwhile
opts.hint: A rival plant makes your parts — and learns your customers.

out.text: Customers are served; a competitor gets a look at your book.
A lost quarter in {city}.

lesson: Single points of failure in a plant are a capital-allocation question: spares and maintenance cost money every year; downtime costs it all at once.

title: Defective batch
text: A batch from your {city} plant has failed in the field. The customer wants every unit from the last two months replaced.

opts.label: Full recall
opts.hint: Replace everything, find the root cause.

out.text: Expensive, thorough, and the customer stays.
Most were fine.
More fail. The customer leaves and tells others.

lesson: Quality failures cost far more in the field than in the factory. A quality system is cheaper than one recall.

title: Serious injury on the line
text: An operator in {city} has been badly hurt by a machine whose guard had been removed to speed up production.

opts.label: Stop the line, full investigation
opts.hint: Find out why the guard was off.

out.text: The investigation finds production targets were the reason. You change them.
The supervisor is fired. Everyone knows the targets have not changed.

lesson: Safety failures are usually incentive failures. Punishing individuals without changing the system guarantees the next accident.

title: They are doing it themselves
text: The retailer has announced its own delivery network. Your contract ends in a quarter.

out.text: A hard year rebuilding volume.

opts.label: Sell them the depots
opts.hint: They need assets; you need cash.

out.text: They buy the depots at a fair price.

lesson: A business built on one customer is that customer’s option, not yours.

title: A serious crash
text: One of your trucks was in a fatal collision near {city}. Early reports suggest the driver had been on the road for fourteen hours.

out.text: A settlement and new rules on hours.
The court agrees.
Your schedules are read out in court.

lesson: Operational pressure shows up as safety risk. Schedules that only work if people break rules are the company’s choice, not the driver’s.

title: Storm damage
text: A storm has torn through the region around {city}. Panels and blades are damaged.

out.text: Back at full output in a quarter.

opts.label: Wait for the insurer
opts.hint: Let them pay before you spend.

out.text: Two quarters of reduced output.

lesson: Physical climate risk is now a balance-sheet item. Resilience costs money, and so does its absence.

title: A partner is leaving — with clients
text: {person}, one of your senior people in {city}, is starting a boutique. Three of your biggest clients have been invited to follow.

out.text: {person} stays.
{person} goes anyway.

opts.label: Call the clients first
opts.hint: Reassure them before the partner does.

out.text: Two of the three stay with you.
They follow the person, not the firm.
Lawyers write letters. Some clients follow anyway.

lesson: In professional services the relationship often belongs to the person, not the firm. Institutionalise client relationships before they walk out the door.

title: Adverse event in the trial
text: A patient in one of your trials has had a serious reaction. The safety board wants to pause enrolment.

out.text: Three months of delay; the trial resumes with new safeguards.
The board agrees; it was unrelated.
A second event follows. Regulators halt the trial.

lesson: In clinical development, safety signals are information. Ignoring them saves a quarter and can cost the programme.

title: A short seller publishes
text: A well-known short seller has published a report calling your lead programme "statistically meaningless".

out.text: The rebuttal holds up; the shares recover.
Analysts find the rebuttal unconvincing.
The shares fall 15% and drift.

lesson: Markets price uncertainty. Transparent data narrows it; silence widens it.

title: Global supply shock
text: A closed shipping lane and a factory fire have created shortages of components everywhere at once.

out.text: You keep shipping, at a cost.
Some customers go short and some leave.

lesson: Lean supply chains are optimised for normal times. Resilience is what you pay for in the year that is not normal.

title: Ransomware
text: Every screen in the company is showing the same message: your files are encrypted, pay within 72 hours.

opts.label: Restore from backups
opts.hint: Days of disruption; no money to criminals.

out.text: The backups work.
The backups were encrypted too.
The keys work.
They ask for more.

lesson: Cyber resilience is backups, drills and segmentation, done before the attack. Paying ransoms funds the next one.

title: A whistleblower
text: An employee has written to the board alleging that sales figures in one region were inflated to hit targets.

out.text: The allegation is upheld; you fix it and restate quietly.
Nothing is found. The process is still respected.

opts.label: Handle it internally
opts.hint: The regional head will look into it.

out.text: It goes away.
The whistleblower goes to the press.

lesson: How a company treats its whistleblowers tells everyone inside it what is really expected.

title: An activist investor
text: A hedge fund has built a 6% stake and published a letter demanding cost cuts and a big buyback.

opts.label: Engage
opts.hint: Meet them and adopt the reasonable parts.

out.text: A cost programme and a modest buyback.
Shareholders back you.
They win two board seats.

lesson: Public companies answer to their shareholders. Activists target companies whose share price lags what their assets could earn.

title: Your biggest customer goes bust
text: Your largest customer has filed for bankruptcy, owing you a quarter of everything on your receivables ledger. Its orders have stopped too.

opts.label: Write it off and chase it in court

out.text: After a year in court you recover a third.
The estate is empty. Nothing comes back.

opts.label: Sell the debt to a collector
opts.hint: A little cash now; the rest is gone.

out.text: A collector pays 25 cents on the dollar.

lesson: Receivables are loans to your customers. Letting one customer owe a large slice of your balance sheet means carrying its risk; credit limits and a spread of customers are the defence.
